items.title: UniSim-Bridge
items.text:
The UniSim-Bridge is a Python framework developed by the PROTEC group of the Polytechnic School of the Federal University of Bahia to automate Honeywell™ UniSim Design Suite® simulations through the Microsoft COM (Component Object Model) protocol.

It allows you to:

  • Open and manipulate a UniSim Desing Suite® .usc case.
  • Advance the dynamic solver in discrete time steps.
  • Inject disturbances or setpoint changes at specific steps into the simulation equipment or into spreadsheets — also known in UniSim's object model as Operations.
  • Persist selected stream, operation, and controller data to a SQLite database.

items.title: Current Structure
items.text:
The framework is currently composed of three main files:

  • setup_subsep.py: Configuration. You edit this to tell the tool which simulation file to open and which operations to track.
  • main.py: The execution script. It loads the setup, runs the simulation loop, and handles cleanup.
  • UnisimConnector.py: The core library. It handles the COM communication, database writing, and object management.

items.title: Who is this for?
items.text: This is for colleagues who are already using the 3-file framework and need a reference for how it works or how to make changes without breaking it.

items.title: What are Operations?
items.text:
In UniSim Design Suite®, an operation is an object that represents a type of equipment in the flowsheet. Valves, compressors, heat exchangers, flash tanks, controllers, pipe segments, heaters, coolers, and spreadsheets. Each operation exposes a set of properties, such as ActuatorPosition, Pressure, or MassFlow, which can be read and written through the COM interface.

Throughout this documentation, when we say "operation", we mean any equipment UniSim exposes on its Flowsheet.Operations collection. The UnisimConnector.py file groups these into Python classes (Valves, Controllers, Compressors, etc.) derived from the Operation superClass, these classes cache the COM objects , record the selected properties at every time step, and persist them to the database.

Full details, class mapping, and the complete list of tracked operation types available in Operations Reference

items.title: Navigating UniSim's COM Object Tree
items.text:
Everything the connector does is a consequence of walking UniSim's COM tree. If you know how to navigate it, you can inspect and modify any object UniSim exposes. See Navigating the COM Object Tree for the full guide — it covers dir(), how to discover properties, and how material streams and subflowsheets are reached.

Start with Installation or jump straight to First Simulation.

items.title: Main.py
items.text:
main.py is the entry point. It holds the logic of one simulation run: open the case, choose what to record, advance the solver step by step, apply changes defined on the script, during the run, and finishing the simulation.

Run it from the project folder:

python main.py

items.title: Execution flow
items.text:
main() has six stages, always in this order:

# Stage Call 1 Configure the run constants at the top of main() 2 Open the case SimulationConnector(...) 3 Declare what to record Simulation.easy_setup(...) 4 (optional) Add properties Simulation.<group>.properties = {...} 5 Validate names and create tables Simulation.build_objects(SUBFLOWSHEETS) 6 Run and close Simulation.update(...) in a loop, then Simulation.finish(...)

Order matters

Properties added in stage 4 must be set before build_objects(). That call builds the property cache and creates the database tables, so a property added afterwards is not recorded.

items.title: 1. Imports and path
items.text:
main.py
script_dir = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
parent_dir = os.path.dirname(script_dir)
sys.path.append(parent_dir)

from UnisimConnector import SimulationConnector
import setup_subsep

The three sys.path lines let Python find UnisimConnector.py when it sits one folder above the script. If UnisimConnector.py is in the same folder as main.py, they are not needed.

script_dir is also used to build output paths, so results are saved next to the script regardless of where you launch Python from.

items.title: 2. Run configuration
items.text:
main.py
## SIMULATION CONFIG ##
OUTPUT_FOLDER = os.path.join(script_dir, 'folder_name') 
DB_NAME = os.path.join(script_dir, 'database_name.db')
# Good Practice is to explain the condition of the simulation on the tag
SIMULATION_TAG = 'opening_valve_condition_130bar70c'  

    # Simulation control
CONTINUE_SIMULATION = False    # Resume from last saved state if True  
SAVE_SIMULATION = False        # Save last simulation state to .usc file when finished 
SHOW_INTERFACE = True          # Display UniSim GUI during execution
EXPORT_CSV = False             # Export the data to csv file
Constant Effect OUTPUT_FOLDER Folder for _simulation_summary.txt, _simulation_properties.txt and CSV files. Created if it does not exist. DB_NAME SQLite file. Several runs can share it, since rows are separated by tag. SIMULATION_TAG Label stored in every row (simulation_tag column). Use a different tag per run that shares the same database. CONTINUE_SIMULATION False resets the solver integrator to its initial state. True continues from the state saved in the .usc. SAVE_SIMULATION True saves the case back to the .usc when the run finishes. SHOW_INTERFACE True shows the UniSim window. False runs hidden, which is useful for long batches. EXPORT_CSV True exports the recorded tables to CSV files when finishing.

items.title: 3. Opening the case and declaring what to record
items.text:
main.py
import os, sys, traceback
from UnisimConnector import SimulationConnector
import setup_subsep

script_dir = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
parent_dir = os.path.dirname(script_dir)
sys.path.append(parent_dir)


Simulation = SimulationConnector(path_unisim, OUTPUT_FOLDER, SIMULATION_TAG,
                                 DB_NAME, CONTINUE_SIMULATION, SHOW_INTERFACE)

Simulation.easy_setup(
    pumps=setup_subsep.PUMPS, valves=setup_subsep.VALVES, flashtanks=setup_subsep.FLASHTANKS,
    compressors=setup_subsep.COMPRESSORS, controllers=setup_subsep.CONTROLLERS,
    heat_exchangers=setup_subsep.HEAT_EXCHANGERS,
    material_streams=setup_subsep.MATERIAL_STREAMS,
    material_streams_phase=setup_subsep.MATERIAL_STREAMS_PHASE,
    heaters=setup_subsep.HEATERS, coolers=setup_subsep.COOLERS, pipes=setup_subsep.PIPES,
    spreadsheets=setup_subsep.SPREADSHEETS,
)

Creating the SimulationConnector launches UniSim (or attaches to it), opens the .usc, and connects to the database. easy_setup() only stores the names. Nothing is read from UniSim until build_objects().

All twelve arguments are required. See setup.py.

items.title: 4. Adding properties that are not recorded by default
items.text:
Each group has a default property list (for example, valves record ActuatorPosition, PressureDrop, MassFlow...). To record more, assign a dictionary of {property: unit}. Assigning merges with the defaults and does not replace them.

main.py
Simulation.controllers.properties = {'Td': 'seconds', 'Ti': 'seconds', 'Gain': ''}

Simulation.heat_exchangers.properties = {
    'Lmtd': 'C',
    'ShellHeatTransferCoef': 'kJ/h-m2-C', 'TubeHeatTransferCoef': 'kJ/h-m2-C',
    'TubeSidePressureDrop': 'bar', 'ShellSidePressureDrop': 'bar',
    'UA': 'kJ/C-h',
}

Simulation.pipes.properties = {
    'SegmentLength': 'm', 'SegmentElevationChange': 'm',
    'SegmentOuterDiam': 'mm', 'SegmentInnerDiam': 'mm',
}
  • Use '' as the unit for dimensionless properties.
  • The new property becomes a new column in the table. If the table already exists in an older database, the column is added automatically (ALTER TABLE).
  • Material streams have three separate dictionaries: properties, phase_properties and components_properties.

The default values and the available groups are listed in Operations and Object Properties.

items.title: 5. Building the objects
items.text:
main.py
try:
    Simulation.build_objects(SUBFLOWSHEETS)
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Initialization failed: {str(e)}")
    traceback.print_exc()
    return

This step checks each configured name against the case, creates the tables and records the initial state (t = 0). Names that cannot be found are removed with a printed message (see troubleshooting).

Debugging breakpoint

The script has a pass line right after the parameters. Put a breakpoint there to inspect Simulation.material_streams.names, Simulation.valves.objects and so on before the loop starts.

items.title: 6. Simulation loop
items.text:
main.py
TIME_STEP_SIZE = 0.033
TIME_STEP_UNIT = 'minutes'
N_SIM_STEPS = 2000

for current_step in range(N_SIM_STEPS):
    ...
    Simulation.update(TIME_STEP_SIZE, TIME_STEP_UNIT)
Parameter Meaning TIME_STEP_SIZE Simulated time advanced per step TIME_STEP_UNIT 'seconds', 'minutes', or 'hr' N_SIM_STEPS Number of steps. Total simulated time is TIME_STEP_SIZE × N_SIM_STEPS (here ≈ 66 minutes)

Minimum step

The UniSim sample time has a lower limit of 2 seconds (≈ 0.033 min). Smaller values are reset to that limit.

Each update() call advances the solver (RunFor) and then writes one row per tracked object to the database.

items.title: Applying disturbances
items.text:
Put changes before Simulation.update(...), so they take effect during that step. Objects are accessed by name:

main.py
if current_step == 3:                                              # after 3 steps
    Simulation.controllers['LIC-100'].SP.SetValue(60, 'bar')       # change a setpoint
    Simulation.valves['VLV-100'].ActuatorPosition.SetValue(100, '%')  # open a valve

Do not use continue for disturbances

The example in the script has if current_step == 3: continue. A continue jumps to the next iteration without calling update(), so that step is not simulated and nothing is recorded for it. Use the if block to change values and let the loop reach update().

Reading and writing follow the same pattern:

Simulation.material_streams['stream_name'].Temperature.GetValue('C')
Simulation.controllers['LIC-100'].PV.GetValue('')
Simulation.valves['VLV-100'].ActuatorPosition.SetValue(50, '%')

If you are unsure about the unit, use GetValue(''). For other ways to explore the UniSim object model, see COM Navigation.

items.title: Error handling
items.text:
main.py
try:
    Simulation.update(TIME_STEP_SIZE, TIME_STEP_UNIT)
except Exception as e:
    simulation_aborted = True
    traceback.print_exc()

An error stops the loop and sets simulation_aborted. The data recorded until that moment is already in the database, because rows are committed at every step.

items.title: 7. Finishing
items.text:
main.py
quit_unisim = not simulation_aborted
Simulation.finish(quit_unisim, SAVE_SIMULATION, EXPORT_CSV)
Outcome quit_unisim Result Completed True UniSim is closed Aborted False UniSim stays open so you can inspect the case

finish() writes the summary and units files, optionally the CSV files, closes the database and (if requested) closes UniSim. Details in UnisimConnector.py.

Pass the arguments in the right order

The signature is finish(quit_unisim, save_simulation, export_csv). Calling finish(quit_unisim, EXPORT_CSV) sends the CSV flag to save_simulation. Keyword arguments avoid this mistake:

Simulation.finish(quit_unisim=True, save_simulation=SAVE_SIMULATION, export_csv=EXPORT_CSV)

items.title: Single-file variant
items.text:
hv50_part1.py shows the same flow with the setup declared inside the script and extra logic for experiments. The differences are:

  • The lists are lowercase variables at the top of the file (valves = [...], spreadsheets = {...}), with no import setup.
  • A for loop over a parameter grid (combvec(bp1_positions, bp2_positions)) creates one SimulationConnector per scenario, each with its own tag (bp1_50.0-bp2_20.0) but the same database.
  • A background timeout monitor thread kills UniSim if a step takes too long (persistent_timeout_monitor, run_simulation_step).
  • slew_rate_filter generates smooth ramps for actuator changes instead of abrupt steps.
  • Each scenario appends a line to simulation_logs.txt (success time or failure) and optionally saves the case with Simulation.case.SaveAs(...).

These helper functions are described in Utilities Functions.

items.title: setup.py
items.text:
setup.py is the configuration file of a simulation project. It contains only constants that answer one question: which objects of the UniSim case should be recorded?

The user must define the names of the Material Streams, Subflowsheets, Spreadsheets, and Equipment they want to monitor, following the rules below

items.title: Names must match the .usc file
items.text:
The names you pass in must match the names as they appear in your .uscfile.

Case does not matter These are all treated as the same name:. 

VALVES = ["VLV-100"]
VALVES = ["vlv-100"]
VALVES = ["vLV-100"]
UniSim-Bridge's existence check ignores case, so either form will find the object.

However special characters, accents, other non-ASCII characters and spacing do matter in practice. Even though the check is case-insensitive, copying names exactly as they appear in the .usc file avoids erros.

For example:

# Space vs. hyphen vs. underscore — three different names:
MATERIALSTREAMS = ['liq sep'] 
MATERIALSTREAMS = ['liq-sep']
MATERIALSTREAMS = ['liq_sep'] 

# Accents and spacing — three more different names:
MATERIALSTREAMS = ['poço de produção'] 
MATERIALSTREAMS = ['poco de producao'] 
MATERIALSTREAMS = ['poço_de_produção']

These may look like variations of the same name, but to UniSim they are different objects:

  • 'liq sep', 'liq-sep', and 'liq_sep' are three separate objects. The space, hyphen, and underscore are not interchangeable.

  • 'poço de produção', 'poco de producao', and 'poço_de_produção' are likewise three separate names. Accents are significant (ç ≠ c, ã ≠ a), and a space is not the same as an underscore.

Tip

To guarantee that a name is correct, use the utility functions to list the names in the open case, or copy the name directly from the .usc file.

items.title: Almost every variable is a list of strings
items.text:
With the exception of spreadsheets, every variable in setup.py follows this shape:

equipment_type: list[str] = ['object_name']

In other words: - The value is always a list, even when it holds a single object or none at all, becoming an empty list. - Each item is a string matching a name in the .usc file (see the previous rule)

The correct way to pass the values are as follows

# Correct — always a list of strings
valves: list[str] = ['VLV-100', 'VLV-101']
flashtanks: list[str] = ['V-100']
material_streams: list[str] = ['feed_sep', 'liq sep', '1']

# Also correct — an empty list when there is nothing to monitor
pumps: list[str] = []
heaters: list[str] = []



# When an object lives inside a subflowsheet, list the subflowsheet in --SUBFLOWSHEETS--. 
# The library searches the main flowsheet first and then each subflowsheet.
SUBFLOWSHEETS = ['TPL1, TPL2']

Incorrect passage

    # Wrong — a bare string, not a list
    valves = 'VLV-100'

    # Wrong — a tuple, not a list
    valves = ('VLV-100',)

    # Wrong — None instead of an empty list
    pumps = None

items.title: Spreadsheets
items.text:
The dictionary maps the spreadsheet name to the cells to read:

SPREADSHEETS = {'RGO': ['B24', 'F24']}   # reads cells B24 and F24 of spreadsheet "RGO"

items.title: Expected Variables in the file
items.text:
Variable Type Content path_unisim str Full path of the .usc case file SUBFLOWSHEETS list[str] Subflowsheets to search for objects (empty list if none) MATERIAL_STREAMS list[str] Material streams to record MATERIAL_STREAMS_PHASE list[str] Streams for which phase-level data is also recorded FLASHTANKS list[str] Flash tanks CONTROLLERS list[str] Feedback controllers VALVES list[str] Valves HEAT_EXCHANGERS list[str] Heat exchangers COMPRESSORS list[str] Compressors PUMPS list[str] Pumps PIPES list[str] Pipe segments HEATERS list[str] Heaters COOLERS list[str] Coolers SPREADSHEETS dict[str, list[str]] {spreadsheet name: [cells]}

Every variable must exist, even when empty

main.py passes all of them to SimulationConnector.easy_setup(), which reads each key directly. A missing key raises a KeyError. When you do not need a category, declare it empty (PUMPS: list[str] = [], SPREADSHEETS: dict[str, list[str]] = {}).

items.title: Example
items.text:
setup_subsep.py
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-

# Raw string (r"...") avoids problems with Windows backslashes
path_unisim = r"C:\path\to\file\simulation.usc"

SUBFLOWSHEETS: list[str] = []

MATERIAL_STREAMS: list[str] = ['feed_sep', 'liq sep', 'gas_sep', 'pump_1_in', 'pump_2_out']
MATERIAL_STREAMS_PHASE: list[str] = ['pump_1_in', 'pump_2_out']

FLASHTANKS: list[str] = ['V-100', 'V-101']
CONTROLLERS: list[str] = ['LIC-100', 'LIC-101', 'LIC-102']
VALVES: list[str] = ['VLV-100', 'VLV-101', 'Valve_bypass_1']
HEAT_EXCHANGERS: list[str] = ['E-100', 'E-100-2']
# 'pump_1' and 'pump_2' are of type compressor in UniSim, so they go here
COMPRESSORS: list[str] = ['pump_1', 'pump_2']

PUMPS: list[str] = []
PIPES: list[str] = []
HEATERS: list[str] = []
COOLERS: list[str] = []

SPREADSHEETS: dict[str, list[str]] = {
    'RGO': ['B24', 'F24'],
    'Pressure_boundary_condition': ['B2'],
}

Note

In this case the equipment named pump_1 and pump_2 are of type compressor in UniSim, so they go in COMPRESSORS, not PUMPS. The name does not matter, the UniSim type does. See Troubleshooting.

items.title: Importing setup on main.py
items.text:
The file can have any name. The example project uses setup_example.py, main.py imports it with:

Explicit Variables NamesImplicit Variable Names on main.py
from setup_example import (
    path_unisim,
    pumps, valves, flashtanks, compressors, controllers,
    heat_exchangers, material_streams, material_streams_phase,
    heaters, coolers, pipes, spreadsheets, subflowsheets,
)
on main.py
import setup_example

Two ways to configure a project

  • Two-file mode (this page): the configuration lives in setup_*.py and the logic in main.py.
  • Single-file mode: the same variables are declared at the top of main.py, as in hv50_part1.py. Nothing else changes, because the library receives the same lists either way. See main.py.

Prefer two files when you reuse one script across several cases, and a single file for one-off experiments or parameter sweeps.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
When build_objects() cannot use a name, it prints a message and removes the name from the list instead of stopping. Check the console on the first run.

Message Cause Fix 'X' not found in <type> list. The name does not exist in the main flowsheet or in the listed subflowsheets Check spelling, or add the subflowsheet to SUBFLOWSHEETS Wrong type for X: expected A, got B The object exists but is of another type Move it to the correct list (e.g. from PUMPS to COMPRESSORS) Access failed for X: ... COM error while reading the object Confirm the object is valid in the open case KeyError: 'pumps' A variable is missing from the setup Declare it as an empty list

items.title: UnisimConnector.py
items.text:
UnisimConnector.py is the library. It connects Python to UniSim Design through COM, reads the properties of the objects you selected at every time step, and stores them in an SQLite database. You normally do not edit it. You import one class from it:

from UnisimConnector import SimulationConnector

Requirements

  • Windows with UniSim Design installed (the library uses win32com).
  • Python packages: pywin32 and pandas. sqlite3 is part of the standard library.
  • Type hints such as list[str] require Python 3.9 or newer.

Authors

Guilherme Ribeiro, Daniel Diniz, Raony Fontes.

items.title: File layout
items.text:
The file is a single module with three layers:

UnisimConnector.py
│
├── binary_search()            utility
│
├── Operation                  base class (shared logic)
│   ├── MaterialStreams        + StreamComponents, MaterialStreams.Phase
│   ├── Valves
│   ├── Pumps
│   ├── Compressors
│   ├── Controllers
│   ├── HeatExchangers
│   ├── Flashtanks
│   ├── Heaters
│   ├── Coolers
│   └── Pipesegs
│
├── Spreadsheets               separate class (not an Operation subclass)
│
└── SimulationConnector        orchestrator, the public entry point
Component Responsibility binary_search Fast name lookup in a sorted list of strings Operation Validates names, caches COM property objects, creates tables, inserts rows, exports CSV MaterialStreams Bulk, component-level and phase-level data of streams StreamComponents Holder of component data (mass/molar flows and fractions) Spreadsheets Reads individual cells of spreadsheet operations Equipment classes Only declare the UniSim type name and the default properties SimulationConnector Opens UniSim, owns all handlers, runs steps, finishes the run

items.title: Operation
items.text: Operation is the base class of every equipment handler. It contains all the shared logic (name validation, property cache, table creation, row insertion, CSV export), so a subclass only declares what to read. The concepts (what an operation is in UniSim, which types exist and which properties they expose) are explained in Operations. This section describes the code.

items.title: Class structure
items.text:
Operation                          shared logic
│
├── Valves           'valveop'
├── Pumps            'pumpop'
├── Compressors      'compressor'
├── Controllers      'fbcontrolop'
├── HeatExchangers   'heatexop'
├── Flashtanks       'flashtank'
├── Heaters          'heaterop'
├── Coolers          'coolerop'
├── Pipesegs         'pipeseg'          overrides _update_data
└── MaterialStreams  'materialstream'   overrides _build_data, _update_data, _save_to_csv

Spreadsheets does not inherit from Operation because it reads cells, not named properties, but it implements the same four methods, so SimulationConnector treats it like the others (see Interface used by the connector).

A subclass defines only:

Member Meaning _operation_title UniSim TypeName of the objects. It is also used as the table name. properties {property: unit} recorded by default.

items.title: Constructor and attributes
items.text:
Operation(db_conn: sqlite3.Connection, db_tag: str, cursor: sqlite3.Cursor)

The connection, the cursor and the tag are shared with the SimulationConnector and with all other handlers.

Attribute Type Content _operation_title str UniSim TypeName. Overridden by each subclass. _names list[str] Names requested in the setup. Exposed as names. objects dict[str, CDispatch] Validated COM objects, keyed by name. _properties dict[str, str] {property: unit}. Exposed as properties. comObjs_properties dict Cache {name: {property: (COM property object, unit)}}. data dict Values read in the most recent step, {name: {'time': t, property: value}}. db_conn, cursor, db_tag Database connection, cursor and run tag. df DataFrame Created by _save_to_csv() after an export. Does not exist before.

items.title: Public interface
items.text:
Member Behavior names Getter returns the list. The setter extends the list (handler.names = [...] appends). properties Getter returns the dictionary. The setter merges (dict.update), so defaults are kept and an existing key gets its unit replaced. handler['VLV-100'] Returns the COM object of a validated name. Raises KeyError if the name is not in objects. get_table_name() Returns _operation_title, except for streams (materialstream_properties).

The object returned by handler['name'] is the live COM object, so it is also how you change values during a run:

Simulation.valves['VLV-100'].ActuatorPosition.SetValue(100, '%')

items.title: Interface used by the connector
items.text:
SimulationConnector drives every handler through the same four methods:

build_objects()   →  handler._build_object(handler.names, operations, subflowsheet_operations)
                  →  handler._build_data(0.0)
update()          →  handler._update_data(time=t)
finish()          →  handler._save_to_csv(output_folder)

The underscore marks these as internal: you rarely call them yourself. Any new class that implements these four methods can be added to the connector.

items.title: Life cycle
items.text:
easy_setup()        names stored in  .names
     │
build_objects()     _build_object()                 validate names → .objects
     │              _build_data(0.0)
     │                ├─ build_properties_cache()   keep COM property objects
     │                ├─ create_operation_table()   CREATE TABLE / ALTER TABLE
     │                └─ _update_data(0.0)          first row (t = 0)
     │
update()            _update_data(t)  ──► _insert_row_to_db()
     │
finish()            _save_to_csv()   (optional)

items.title: _build_object()
items.text:
_build_object(name_list, unisim_operation_object, unisim_subflow_op_object) -> None

Validates the requested names against the case and fills objects.

  1. Builds a sorted list of the upper-cased names of the main flowsheet and looks each requested name up with binary_search (so the check is case-insensitive).
  2. If found, it checks that the object's TypeName matches _operation_title and stores the COM object. A mismatch prints Wrong type for X: expected A, got B.
  3. If not found, it tries each subflowsheet collection in order. If every attempt fails (or there are no subflowsheets), it prints 'X' not found in <type> list.
  4. Names that failed are removed from name_list in place. Because the connector passes handler.names, afterwards names contains only valid names.

items.title: build_properties_cache()
items.text:
For each valid object and each property, it fetches the COM property object once (getattr(obj, prop_name)) and stores it with its unit in comObjs_properties. Each later step then only calls GetValue(unit). The authors report a 150% speed-up in data collection from this cache, because every attribute lookup crosses the Python/COM boundary.

A property that does not exist on the object

If getattr fails, the property is skipped silently and is absent from the cache. The step then has no value for it, and _insert_row_to_db() raises a KeyError for that property. In practice, a misspelled or unsupported property name fails during build_objects(). Check the exact name in the case before adding it (see COM Navigation).

items.title: _build_data()
items.text:
_build_data(time: float) -> None

Initializes the recording: builds the property cache, creates (or evolves) the table, and records the first row.

items.title: _update_data()
items.text:
_update_data(time: float) -> None

Reads every cached property with GetValue(unit) and stores the result in data. A value that cannot be read is stored as None (NULL in the database) and the run continues. After each object, it calls _insert_row_to_db(self.data).

Repeated writes

The insert is called inside the loop over objects and receives the whole data dictionary, so earlier objects are written again for each new object. The upsert makes this harmless for the data, but it means roughly n(n+1)/2 row writes per step for n objects, each followed by a commit.

items.title: _insert_row_to_db()
items.text:
_insert_row_to_db(data: dict) -> None

Writes one row per object with the columns name, time, simulation_tag, date and one column per property.

  • time is formatted with four decimals (:.4f) and date is the current day as dd-mm-yyyy.
  • It is an upsert: a repeated (name, time, simulation_tag) overwrites the property values.
  • It commits at the end.

A handler with objects but no properties fails

The upsert clause is built from the property names. With an empty properties dictionary (the default of Pumps), the generated SQL is incomplete and build_objects() raises sqlite3.OperationalError: incomplete input. If you list pumps, add at least one property first (for example Simulation.pumps.properties = {'Energy': 'kW'}). An empty PUMPS list is fine.

items.title: create_operation_table()
items.text: Creates the table if needed, with name TEXT, time REAL, simulation_tag TEXT, date TEXT and one REAL column per property, with primary key (name, time, simulation_tag). It then compares the table with properties and runs ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN for each missing property, printing new column added to <table> <property>. This is what allows a database from an earlier run to accept new properties.

items.title: _save_to_csv()
items.text:
_save_to_csv(output_folder: str) -> None

Selects all columns except simulation_tag for the current tag, builds a DataFrame indexed by name, keeps it in self.df and writes <output_folder><TAG>_<table>_data.csv. Nothing is written when there are no rows. The path is built by concatenation, so the folder must end with a separator.

items.title: Overridden behavior
items.text:
Pipesegs replaces _update_data(). It reads GetValue and, if the property is a vector (segment properties such as SegmentLength), falls back to GetValues and stores the sum of the segments. A sum makes sense for lengths and elevation changes, not for diameters.

Verify pipes before relying on them

Pipesegs._update_data() stores one-row DataFrames in data, while _insert_row_to_db() formats data_['time'] with :.4f, which pandas does not support for a Series (TypeError). From reading the code, listing a pipe is likely to fail at build_objects(). Neither example script lists pipes (PIPES = []), so this path is untested. Check it on a case with pipes before using it.

MaterialStreams overrides _build_data(), _update_data() and _save_to_csv() to add component and phase data. See MaterialStreams.

Spreadsheets implements its own versions of the four methods, with a {spreadsheet: [cells]} dictionary in place of names. See Spreadsheets.

items.title: Equipment classes
items.text:
Each class is a few lines: it sets _operation_title (the UniSim TypeName) and the default properties ({name: unit}). Everything else is inherited from Operation.

Attribute of SimulationConnector Class UniSim TypeName Default properties Table valves Valves valveop ActuatorPosition, PressureDrop, FeedTemperature, FeedPressure, MolarFlow, MassFlow valveop pumps Pumps pumpop (none) pumpop compressors Compressors compressor MassFlow, FeedTemperature, FeedPressure, CompressorSpeed, CompAdiabaticEff, AdiabaticHead, Energy, PressureIncrease compressor controllers Controllers fbcontrolop SP, PV, OP, RampDuration fbcontrolop heat_exchangers HeatExchangers heatexop Duty heatexop flashtanks Flashtanks flashtank VesselPressure, VesselTemperature flashtank heaters Heaters heaterop MassFlow, FeedTemperature, FeedPressure, ProductTemperature heaterop coolers Coolers coolerop MassFlow, FeedTemperature, FeedPressure, ProductTemperature coolerop pipes Pipesegs pipeseg PressureDrop pipeseg material_streams MaterialStreams materialstream see MaterialStreams materialstream_properties spreadsheets Spreadsheets spreadsheetop cells chosen in the setup spreadsheet_<NAME>

Pumps have no default properties

Pumps starts with an empty property list. Listing a pump without adding at least one property makes build_objects() fail (see _insert_row_to_db()). Add what you need before build_objects():

Simulation.pumps.properties = {'Energy': 'kW'}

The complete reference of default properties and units is in Operations.

items.title: MaterialStreams
items.text:
MaterialStreams records the state of the material streams of the flowsheet. It is the most detailed handler of the library, because a stream carries information at three levels: the stream as a whole, its components, and each of its phases. It is available as Simulation.material_streams.

Unlike the equipment classes, streams are searched in Flowsheet.Streams (and in the Streams collection of each subflowsheet), not in Flowsheet.Operations.

items.title: Three levels of data
items.text:
Level Dictionary Default content Tables Bulk properties Pressure, StdGasFlow, MassFlow, MolarFlow, StdLiqVolFlow, Temperature, MassDensity, VapourFraction, ActualGasFlow, ActualLiqFlow, ActualVolumeFlow materialstream_properties Components components_properties ComponentMassFlow, ComponentMolarFlow, ComponentMolarFraction, ComponentMassFraction materialstream_components Phases phase_properties MassFlow, MolarFlow, MassDensity, ActualVolumeFlow, Viscosity, PhaseFraction <phase>_properties and <phase>_components

The three phases are VapourPhase, LightLiquidPhase and HeavyLiquidPhase, so the phase tables are vapourphase_properties, vapourphase_components, lightliquidphase_properties, lightliquidphase_components, heavyliquidphase_properties and heavyliquidphase_components.

Phase data is only collected for the streams listed in material_streams_phase (stored in collected_phases). It is the heaviest part of the collection, so request it only where you need it.

items.title: How each level is stored
items.text:
Bulk properties are scalars, handled exactly like any other operation: one row per stream and time, with one column per property.

Components are vectors with one value per chemical component. They are read with GetValues(unit) and stored in materialstream_components with one column per component and one row per property:

stream_name time simulation_tag property_type Methane Ethane ... feed_sep 0.033 teste ComponentMassFlow 120.4 35.1 ... feed_sep 0.033 teste ComponentMolarFraction 0.71 0.19 ...

Phases follow the same idea. The phase property tables have one column per property (stream_name, time, simulation_tag, MassFlow, ...). The phase component tables use property_type with the values MassFractions and MolarFractions, and one column per component.

Component names

The component columns come from the fluid package of the first valid stream. All recorded streams are assumed to share the same fluid package.

items.title: Customizing the properties
items.text:
Each dictionary accepts additions in the same way as the equipment handlers: assigning merges with the existing entries.

Simulation.material_streams.properties = {'Temperature': 'K'}            # bulk
Simulation.material_streams.phase_properties = {'Temperature': 'K'}      # per phase
Simulation.material_streams.components_properties = {'ComponentMolarFraction': ''}

Assigning a key that already exists replaces its unit.

Set properties before build_objects()

The COM property objects are cached and the tables are created inside build_objects(). Changes made afterwards are ignored.

Units are not stored in the database

The tables have no unit column. If you change a unit and reuse the same database, values of different runs will be mixed with no marker. Each run writes the units it used to _simulation_properties.txt, and a new tag per unit configuration keeps runs distinguishable.

items.title: Reading the data
items.text:
import sqlite3, pandas as pd
conn = sqlite3.connect('db_name1.db')

# Bulk
bulk = pd.read_sql(
    "SELECT time, Temperature, MassFlow FROM materialstream_properties "
    "WHERE name = 'feed_sep' AND simulation_tag = 'teste' ORDER BY time", conn)

# Components of the stream
comps = pd.read_sql(
    "SELECT * FROM materialstream_components "
    "WHERE stream_name = 'feed_sep' AND property_type = 'ComponentMolarFraction' "
    "AND simulation_tag = 'teste' ORDER BY time", conn)

# One phase
vapour = pd.read_sql(
    "SELECT time, MassFlow, Viscosity FROM vapourphase_properties "
    "WHERE stream_name = 'pump_1_in' AND simulation_tag = 'teste' ORDER BY time", conn)

Note that the bulk table identifies the stream in the name column, while the components and phase tables use stream_name. See Database Tables.

items.title: Behavior to be aware of
items.text:
• A property that cannot be read (for example, the viscosity of a phase that does not exist in that stream) is stored as NULL. The run continues.
  • At least one valid stream is required. The library reads the component list from the first stream in objects. If every name is rejected, build_objects() fails at this point.
  • The bulk and phase property tables are upserted (a repeated (stream, time, tag) overwrites the row). The component tables use INSERT OR IGNORE, so a repeated key keeps the old values. When you rerun with the same database, use a new tag.

items.title: Spreadsheets
items.text: Spreadsheets is not an Operation subclass because it reads cells, not named properties. The setup is {spreadsheet: [cells]}. At each step it reads Cell(cell).CellValue and stores one row per cell in a table named spreadsheet_<NAME> (name in upper case) with the columns cell, time, simulation_tag, date, value.

items.title: SimulationConnector
items.text: The only class most users need.

items.title: Creating the connector
items.text:
SimulationConnector(file_path_unisim, OUTPUT_FOLDER, db_tag,
                    db_name='Simulation.db',
                    continue_simulation=True, case_visible=True)
Argument Description file_path_unisim Path of the .usc file OUTPUT_FOLDER Folder for text and CSV outputs (created if missing) db_tag Label of this run, stored in every row db_name SQLite file continue_simulation False resets the integrator, True keeps the saved state case_visible Show or hide the UniSim window

The constructor, in order:

  1. Opens the SQLite connection and sets synchronous = NORMAL, journal_mode = WAL and a ~256 MB cache, which favors fast writes during long runs.
  2. Creates OUTPUT_FOLDER if needed.
  3. Starts UniSim (UnisimDesign.Application), opens the case and sets its visibility.
  4. Stores the UniSim process id in process_id and gets the solver integrator (Solver.Integrator) as integrador, with Mode = 0. The integrator is reset when continue_simulation is False.
  5. Creates one handler per operation type (material_streams, valves, pumps, pipes, heat_exchangers, compressors, controllers, flashtanks, coolers, heaters, spreadsheets).

operations list

Simulation.operations holds the equipment handlers only. material_streams and spreadsheets are handled separately by the library because their data structures differ.

items.title: Main methods
items.text: Method When What it does easy_setup(**kwargs) After creating Stores the names to record build_objects(subFlowsheet=[]) After setup Validates names, creates tables, records t = 0 update(sample_time, time_unit, id) Every step Advances the solver and records one row per object finish(quit_unisim, save_simulation, export_csv) End Writes summary files, closes database and UniSim

items.title: Finishing a run
items.text: A run ends with Simulation.finish(...). It closes the loop that started with SimulationConnector(...): it writes the documentation files of the run, optionally exports the data, and releases the database and UniSim.

items.title: Sequence
items.text:
1. Summary file: writes _simulation_summary.txt with the case file name and, for each group, the objects that were actually found. This is the quickest way to confirm which names survived the validation of build_objects().
  2. Units file: writes _simulation_properties.txt with every tracked property and its unit, per operation type (and per level for material streams).
  3. CSV export (only if export_csv=True): writes one file per table, filtered by the current tag, as <TAG>_<table>_data.csv.
  4. Database: closes the SQLite connection.
  5. UniSim (only if quit_unisim=True): closes the case and quits the application.

Errors in steps 1 to 3 are printed with a traceback but do not prevent the following steps. The database is always closed.

items.title: Output files
items.text: File Always written Content _simulation_summary.txt yes Case name and objects found per group _simulation_properties.txt yes Tracked properties and units <TAG>_<table>_data.csv only with export_csv=True Table content for this tag (simulation_tag excluded) *.db created at start All recorded data, always available even without CSV export

items.title: Closing behavior
items.text:
Situation quit_unisim save_simulation Result Normal end True True Case saved, UniSim closed Normal end True False Case closed without saving, UniSim closed Normal end, keep it open False any UniSim stays open (useful for debugging) Run aborted by an error False (recommended) ignored UniSim stays open so you can inspect the state

When save_simulation is None (the default), the library saves only if the run was created with continue_simulation=True. This makes a continue workflow save its state automatically, while a first run does not overwrite the original case.

The _simulation_abort flag

The connector has an internal flag, _simulation_abort, initialized to False. When it is True and quit_unisim=True, finish() does not close the case normally and instead terminates UniSim with taskkill /f /im unisimdesign.exe, which closes every UniSim process on the machine. The library itself never sets this flag, so the branch is only reached if your own code sets it. For ordinary errors, pass quit_unisim=False and close UniSim yourself.

items.title: Recommended pattern
items.text:
aborted = False
for step in range(N_SIM_STEPS):
    try:
        Simulation.update(TIME_STEP_SIZE, TIME_STEP_UNIT)
    except Exception:
        traceback.print_exc()
        aborted = True
        break

Simulation.finish(
    quit_unisim=not aborted,
    save_simulation=SAVE_SIMULATION,
    export_csv=EXPORT_CSV,
)

Trailing separator in OUTPUT_FOLDER

CSV paths are built by concatenating OUTPUT_FOLDER and the file name. End the folder path with a separator (os.path.join(folder, '')), as explained in main.py.

items.title: Functions
items.text: Reference of the public methods of SimulationConnector. The usual order of a run is easy_setup() → build_objects() → update() (repeated) → finish().

items.title: Easy_Setup()
items.text:
easy_setup(**kwargs) -> None

Declares what to record. It receives one list of names per operation type, validates them and stores them in the handlers. It does not talk to UniSim: nothing is checked against the case until build_objects().

items.title: Arguments
items.text:
All twelve keyword arguments are required, even when empty.

Argument Type Handler that receives it pumps list[str] pumps valves list[str] valves flashtanks list[str] flashtanks compressors list[str] compressors controllers list[str] controllers heat_exchangers list[str] heat_exchangers material_streams list[str] material_streams material_streams_phase list[str] material_streams (subset with phase data) heaters list[str] heaters coolers list[str] coolers pipes list[str] pipes spreadsheets dict[str, list[str]] spreadsheets ({name: [cells]})

items.title: What it does
items.text:
1. Validates the types. A list of strings is expected for every argument except spreadsheets, which must be a dictionary of lists. Other types (a tuple or a set, for example) or non-string items raise TypeError.
  2. Removes duplicates by converting each list to a set. The original order is lost.
  3. Merges the stream lists. material_streams receives the union of material_streams and material_streams_phase, and collected_phases receives material_streams_phase. A stream that needs phase data therefore does not have to be listed twice.
  4. Stores the names in each handler (Simulation.valves.names, ...) and the cell map in Simulation.spreadsheets.cells.

items.title: Example
items.text:
Simulation.easy_setup(
    pumps=[],
    valves=['VLV-100', 'VLV-101'],
    flashtanks=['V-100'],
    compressors=['pump_1', 'pump_2'],
    controllers=['LIC-100'],
    heat_exchangers=['E-100'],
    material_streams=['feed_sep', 'gas_sep'],
    material_streams_phase=['pump_1_in'],      # also added to material_streams
    heaters=[],
    coolers=[],
    pipes=[],
    spreadsheets={'RGO': ['B24', 'F24']},
)

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• Missing argument: raises KeyError (for example KeyError: 'pumps'). Pass an empty list instead.
  • Call it once. Each call appends to the handlers' name lists, so a second call duplicates names. The spreadsheet map and collected_phases are replaced instead.
  • Names in the wrong place are not detected here. A valve listed under pumps is only reported by build_objects().
  • The usual source of these lists is the setup file.

items.title: Build_Objects()
items.text:
build_objects(subFlowsheet=[]) -> None

Connects the names declared in easy_setup() to the real objects in the case. For each name it searches the main flowsheet and then the subflowsheets in subFlowsheet, checks the UniSim type, and discards names that are missing or of the wrong type (with a printed message). Then it builds the property caches, creates the tables and records the t = 0 row.

Argument Description subFlowsheet Names of subflowsheets to search (e.g. ['ColumnSubFlowsheet']). Defaults to none.

Add custom properties before calling it. See main.py.

items.title: Update()
items.text:
update(sample_time=None, time_unit=None, id=None) -> None

Advances the solver and records one row per tracked object.

Call Behavior update(1.0, 'hr') Runs the solver for the interval (RunFor), then records at the new solver time update(id=10) Records at the given identifier without advancing the solver

Numeric time or id

The time column is written with a fixed numeric format (:.4f), so id must be a number. Calling update() with no arguments is not supported in the current version for the same reason: the time would be an empty string.

items.title: Finish()
items.text:
finish(quit_unisim=True, save_simulation=None, export_csv=False) -> None

Writes the run files, optionally exports CSV, closes the database and (optionally) UniSim. The full behavior, including the closing scenarios, is described in Finishing a run.

Argument Description quit_unisim Close the case and quit UniSim when True save_simulation Save the case when closing. None follows continue_simulation export_csv Export every tracked table to CSV

items.title: Discovery helpers
items.text:
Use them to list the real names and types in a case. They query UniSim and do not depend on the setup.

Method Returns get_material_streams() Sorted list of stream names get_valves(), get_pumps(), get_compressors(), get_controllers(), get_heatexchangers(), get_flashtanks(), get_spreadsheets() Names of that operation type get_subflowsheets() [(Name, TaggedName), ...] get_all_operations() {TypeName: [names]} for every operation in the flowsheet

There are no dedicated helpers for pipes, heaters and coolers. Use get_all_operations() for those.

items.title: Custom database methods
items.text:
The connector also exposes generic helpers to store your own data (experiment notes, derived metrics) in the same database:

Method Purpose create_table(table_name, columns, primary_keys=None) Create a table from column definitions add_columns(table_name, columns) Add columns to an existing table insert_row(table_name, data, conflict_columns=None, update_columns=None) Insert, with optional upsert update_row(table_name, data, condition_columns) Update rows matching the condition columns query_table(table_name, conditions=None, order_by=None, limit=None) Select rows, returns a list get_table_info(table_name) Column information of a table

items.title: Database
items.text:
One SQLite file holds every run. Rows are separated by the simulation_tag column and upserted on (name, time, simulation_tag), so recording the same time twice for the same tag overwrites instead of duplicating.

Common columns of the equipment tables:

Column Content name Object name time Solver time (in the unit used in update) simulation_tag Run label date Run date (dd-mm-yyyy) one column per property Recorded value (REAL)

Schema changes are automatic: when you add a property, the library adds the missing column to existing tables.

Example query with pandas:

import sqlite3, pandas as pd

conn = sqlite3.connect('db_name1.db')
df = pd.read_sql(
    "SELECT time, ActuatorPosition, MassFlow "
    "FROM valveop WHERE name = 'VLV-100' AND simulation_tag = 'teste' ORDER BY time",
    conn,
)

items.title: Extending the library
items.text:
To support a new UniSim operation type, add a class in the same style as the existing ones:

class MyOperations(Operation):
    def __init__(self, db_conn, db_tag, cursor):
        super().__init__(db_conn, db_tag, cursor)
        self._operation_title = '<TypeName>'   # UniSim TypeName of the object
        self.properties = dict(
            # PropertyName='unit',
        )

Then, inside SimulationConnector:

  1. Create the handler in __init__ (self.my_operations = MyOperations(...)) and add it to self.operations.
  2. Read its names in easy_setup.
  3. Add a line for it in the summary written by finish().

Use get_all_operations() to discover the TypeName of the new object.

items.title: Known limitations
items.text:
• Windows only, with UniSim installed (COM).
  • easy_setup() requires every argument, even when empty.
  • build_objects(subFlowsheet=[]) uses a mutable default argument. This is harmless today, because the list is never modified, but passing the list explicitly is safer.
  • Names are de-duplicated through sets, so the original order is lost.
  • The module is a single file. This is deliberate for the current version and is expected to be split into a package in a later one.
  • A pump listed without any property raises an SQL error in build_objects().
  • Pipe segments (Pipesegs) are likely to fail when listed. The code path is not exercised by the example scripts.
  • Operation._update_data() rewrites earlier objects for each new object in the same step, which scales quadratically with the number of objects of a type.

items.title: First Simulation
items.text: the complete project contains three files: setup.py, which declares which objects of the .usc case to monitor, main.py, which opens the case, builds those objects, steps the simulation, and finishes the simulation and UnisimConnector.py.

items.title: Minimal template
items.text:
This template shows the smallest complete main.py — open the case, declare which objects to monitor, build them, step the simulation, and finish the programm. Every name passed to easy_setup() and build_objects comes from setup.py; the full explanation of how it works is available in UnisimConnector.py.

main.py
import os, sys, traceback
from UnisimConnector import SimulationConnector
import setup_subsep

def main():
    here = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
    sim = SimulationConnector(setup_subsep.path_unisim, os.path.join(here, 'out', ''),
                              'run01', os.path.join(here, 'run.db'),
                              continue_simulation=False, case_visible=True)
    sim.easy_setup(
        pumps=setup_subsep.PUMPS, valves=setup_subsep.VALVES, flashtanks=setup_subsep.FLASHTANKS, compressors=setup_subsep.COMPRESSORS,
        controllers=setup_subsep.CONTROLLERS, heat_exchangers=setup_subsep.HEAT_EXCHANGERS,
        material_streams=setup_subsep.MATERIAL_STREAMS, material_streams_phase=setup_subsep.MATERIAL_STREAMS_PHASE,
        heaters=setup_subsep.HEATERS, coolers=setup_subsep.COOLERS, pipes=setup_subsep.PIPES, spreadsheets=setup_subsep.SPREADSHEETS,
    )
    sim.build_objects(setup_subsep.SUBFLOWSHEETS)

    aborted = False
    for step in range(100):
        try:
            sim.update(0.033, 'minutes')
        except Exception:
            traceback.print_exc()
            aborted = True
            break

    sim.finish(quit_unisim=not aborted, save_simulation=False, export_csv=True)

    pass # add a debug break point here 
if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• UniSim Design installed and licensed on your machine.
  • Python 3.13.9 – 3.13.15 (tested; other versions may work but are untested).

items.title: Python Dependencies
items.text:
The framework relies on two external libraries. Install them via pip:

pip install pywin32 pandas
Other libraries

sqlite3 and os are part of Python's standard library — no separate install needed.

items.title: Navigating the COM Object Tree
items.text:
To automate UniSim Design, Python needs a way to talk to it. Because they are completely different software programs, they cannot share memory directly.

Instead, they communicate using the Microsoft Component Object Model (COM).

items.title: How COM Works
items.text:
COM is a binary interoperability standard. It allows software components written in different languages to interact without needing to know each other's internal code.

In COM, you never manipulate the raw memory of the target application. Instead, the target application (UniSim) exposes "objects." These objects provide sets of methods (functions you can call, like .Open()) and properties (values you can read or write, like .Temperature).

To make this work in Python, this framework uses the pywin32 library. It acts as a bridge, handling the complex, low-level allocation of pointers and data types. It lets you treat UniSim's COM objects as if they were normal Python objects.

items.title: The Root Object
items.text:
Everything starts by asking the Windows operating system for a running (or new) instance of UniSim:

import win32com.client as winclt

# Grab the application object
unisim = winclt.Dispatch("UnisimDesign.Application")

# Open a specific case
case = unisim.SimulationCases.Open(r"C:\path\to\your\case.usc")

From this root object, you can navigate down the tree into the flowsheet, the operations, the streams, and the solver.

items.title: Finding Object Values
items.text:
Because COM objects are dynamic, your code editor won't always know what methods and properties exist. You discover them at runtime using Python's built-in dir() function.

If you want to know what equipment is present in the simulation, you can ask the Flowsheet object for the names of all its Operations:

for name in Simulation.case.Flowsheet.Operations.Names:
    print(f'{name, Simulation.case.Flowsheet.Operations[name].TypeName}')

# or you can use the built-in function
Simulation.get_all_operations()

If you want to know what properties a specific object has, pass it to dir():

valve = Simulation.case.Flowsheet.Operations.Item('VLV-100')
dir(valve)

items.title: Subflowsheets
items.text:
Large simulations are often organized into subflowsheets.

Subflowsheets are not stored in the main Flowsheet.Operations list. They are stored in their own collection on the Flowsheet object.

To see a list of all subflowsheets in a case:

print(Simulation.case.Flowsheet.Flowsheets.Names)

To access the equipment inside a subflowsheet, you have to navigate down into it first:

# Get the subflowsheet object
sub_flow = Simulation.case.Flowsheet.Flowsheets.Item('SubFlowsheet1')

# Now you can access its operations and streams
for name in sub_flow.Operations.Names:
    print(name)

Config on setup.py

you must explicitly list the names of any subflowsheets you want to search in the SUBFLOWSHEETS list

items.title: See Also
items.text:
Microsoft COM Technical Overview — A classic introduction to the architecture that powers this framework.

COM Fundamentals — COM underlying architecture

pywin32 Documentation — The Python package that makes the COM connection possible.

items.title: How UniSim-Bridge represents operations
items.text:
UniSim-Bridge wraps each operation type in a Python class derived from Operation. These classes cache the COM objects, record selected properties at every time step, and upload the values to the SQLite database.

The base class lives in UnisimConnector.py as Operation. Each subclass (e.g., Valves, Controllers) only has to declare two things: 1. Its _operation_title (which matches UniSim's TypeName). 2. Its default properties dictionary (which properties to read and in what units).

items.title: The Operation Base Class
items.text: Because all operation classes inherit from the base Operation class, understanding the base class means understanding how every piece of tracked equipment behaves.

items.title: 1. Tracking the Configuration (names)
items.text: When easy_setup() runs, it populates the _names list. You can interact with this list using the .names property. The setter extends the list, allowing you to add new targets programmatically. It removes duplicates via sets before assigning.

items.title: 2. Building and Validating Objects (_build_object)
items.text:
Before data can be collected, _build_object() must find the actual UniSim COM objects. It does this by: - Checking the main flowsheet's Operations collection. - Checking any requested subflowsheets. - Verifying the object's TypeName matches the class's _operation_title. - Storing the valid COM objects in the self.objects dictionary.

If an object is not found or has the wrong type, it prints a warning (e.g., 'VLV-100' not found in valveop list) and removes it from the tracking list so it doesn't cause errors later.

items.title: 3. The Performance Cache (build_properties_cache)
items.text:
In COM, fetching a property object (like valve.ActuatorPosition) is slow. Doing it every time step for every valve creates a massive bottleneck.

To solve this, build_properties_cache() runs once before the simulation loop. It looks up the COM object for every property of every tracked item and saves it in a dictionary called comObjs_properties. During the time-stepping loop, the code simply calls .GetValue(unit) on these pre-fetched objects, resulting in a massive performance improvement (up to 150% faster).

items.title: 4. Data Collection and Persistence (_update_data & _insert_row_to_db)
items.text:
At every time step, _update_data(time) is called. It loops through the cached properties, reads the current value, and builds a dictionary of the data.

It then passes this dictionary to _insert_row_to_db(), which uses an SQL INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE statement. This "upsert" logic means that if a simulation crashes and restarts on the same time step, it will just overwrite the existing row rather than failing or creating duplicates.

items.title: 5. Schema Evolution (create_operation_table)
items.text: The create_operation_table() method handles database initialization. It creates the table based on the properties dictionary. Crucially, if you add a new property to the class in UnisimConnector.py later, the method detects that the column is missing from the existing database and uses ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN to safely update the schema without deleting your existing simulation data.

items.title: The _operation_title → TypeName match
items.text:
Each subclass sets _operation_title to the exact string UniSim uses as an operation's TypeName. That's how _build_object() knows which entries in Flowsheet.Operations belong to which class: it looks up the object, reads its TypeName, and rejects it if it doesn't match.

You can inspect this raw mapping for any open simulation case using a simple Python loop:

TypeName (UniSim) Python class Default properties materialstream MaterialStreams Pressure, Temperature, MassFlow, VapourFraction valveop Valves ActuatorPosition, PressureDrop compressor Compressors CompressorSpeed, AdiabaticEff, Energy heatexop HeatExchangers Duty flashtank Flashtanks VesselPressure, VesselTemperature fbcontrolop Controllers SP, PV, OP pipeseg Pipesegs PressureDrop heaterop Heaters ProductTemperature, FeedTemperature coolerop Coolers ProductTemperature, FeedTemperature spreadsheetop Spreadsheets (user-defined cells) see how to collect spreadsheet data in

The full, current property list for each type is on Object Properties.

items.title: Material streams are a special case
items.text:
MaterialStreams is not stored under Flowsheet.Operations — it's a parallel collection on Flowsheet.MaterialStreams. This is why setup_subsep.py has both MATERIAL_STREAMS and OPERATIONS-style lists: they map to two different UniSim collections, even though they end up in the same SQLite database.

MaterialStreams also does more than the other classes: it records bulk stream properties, per-component flows and fractions, and — for streams listed in MATERIAL_STREAMS_PHASE — per-phase properties. See UnisimConnector.py for the class map.

items.title: Finding Properties
items.text: Once your simulation is running (using the minimal template), you will need to know the exact names of the properties you want to track or change.

items.title: Discovering Property Names
items.text:
Every UniSim object (valves, streams, controllers, etc.) exposes the properties of that family of Operations. You can use the built-in Python dir() function to list them all.

For example, to see what properties every valve has:

dir(Simulation.valves['VLV-101'])

The output is a long list containing every property and method available for Valves:

['ActuatorHasFailed',
 'ActuatorMaximum',
 'ActuatorMaximumValue',
 'ActuatorMinimum',
 'ActuatorMinimumValue',
 'ActuatorMode',
 'ActuatorPosition',
 'ActuatorPositionValue',
 'ActuatorRate',
 'ActuatorRateValue',
 'ActuatorSP',
 ...,
 'PercentOpen' ]

You can use the exact string names from this list (like 'PercentOpen') to track properties beyond the defaults. To do this, add them to your main.py file by following this guide.

items.title: Reading and Writing Values
items.text: Once you know the property name, you interact with it using .GetValue('unit') and .SetValue(value, unit). For dimensionless values, pass an empty string '' as the unit.

items.title: Inputs vs. Outputs (Blue vs. Black)
items.text:
Before trying to change a property via Python, look at it in the UniSim interface:

Blue values are user inputs (specifications). You can change them using .SetValue(value, 'unit').

Black values are calculated outputs. They are read-only. You can read them with .GetValue(value, 'unit'), but attempting to .SetValue() them will throw a COM error.

items.title: Example: Changing a Writeable Value (Valve)
items.text:
In the image below, the Percent Open field is written in blue. This means it is an input that the simulation uses to calculate the rest of the valve's behavior. You can use Python to override this value dynamically during the run.

# Read the current valve position
Simulation.valves['VLV-101'].PercentOpen.GetValue('')
# Output: 50.0

# Force the valve to 30% open
Simulation.valves['VLV-101'].PercentOpen.SetValue(30, '')

# Verify the change
Simulation.valves['VLV-101'].PercentOpen.GetValue('')
# Output: 30.0

items.title: Example: Reading Calculated Values (Stream)
items.text:
In the image below, the stream properties (like Mass Flow) are written in black. These are the results of the simulation's calculations. You cannot set these directly — if you want to change the mass flow, you must change a blue input elsewhere (like a pump speed or valve position).

However, you can freely read them, and UniSim will automatically convert the units for you based on the string you pass:

# Get the mass flow in kilograms per hour
Simulation.material_streams['1'].MassFlow.GetValue('kg/h')
# Output: 149542.36856587604

# Get the exact same mass flow, but converted to pounds per hour
Simulation.material_streams['1'].MassFlow.GetValue('lb/hr')
# Output: 329681.10574033036

See Also Utilities Functions — use get_all_operations() to discover the names of every object in your case.

Navigating the COM Object — how to explore deeper COM objects with dir().

items.title: Utilities Functions
items.text:
These class lives in UnisimConnector.py as Operation. Each subclass (e.g., Valves, Controllers) only has to declare two things:

When configuring setup.py, it is often tedious to manually type out every valve, pump, or stream name. SimulationConnector provides a set of "getter" methods that scan the open UniSim case and return lists of available names for you.

These functions are available on your Simulation object in main.py, after SimulationConnector has been initialized (i.e., after the case is open).

items.title: Discovering Operations by Type
items.text:
You can get a list of names for a specific type of equipment using these methods:

Method Returns Simulation.get_valves() All objects names with TypeName == 'valveop' Simulation.get_pumps() All objects names with TypeName == 'pumpop' Simulation.get_compressors() All objects names with TypeName == 'compressor' Simulation.get_heatexchangers() All objects names with TypeName == 'heatexop' Simulation.get_flashtanks() All objects names with TypeName == 'flashtank' Simulation.get_controllers() All objects names with TypeName == 'fbcontrolop' Simulation.get_spreadsheets() All objects names with TypeName == 'spreadsheetop'

items.title: Discovering Streams and Subflowsheets
items.text:
• Simulation.get_material_streams() — Returns a sorted list of all material stream names.
  • Simulation.get_subflowsheets() — Returns a list of tuples: (Name, TaggedName) for every subflowsheet, as subflowsheets have a user defined Name but the simulator only sees the TaggedName for accessing it.

items.title: Discovering Everything
items.text:
If you want a complete map of the simulation, use:

  • Simulation.get_all_operations() — Returns a dictionary where the keys are the TypeName strings (e.g., 'valveop', 'mixerop') and the values are lists of object names belonging to that type.
ops = Simulation.get_all_operations()

# Get all valves
print(ops['valveop'])
# Output: ['VLV-100', 'VLV-101', 'VLV-102', ...]

# Print the whole dictionary
print(ops)

{
    'valveop': ['VLV-100', 'VLV-101', 'VLV-102', 'VLV-103', 'VLV-104', 'VLV-107', 'VLV-109', 'VLV-111', 'VLV-110', 'VLV-110-2', 'Valve_bypass_1', 'Valve_heat_1', 'VLV-106', 'Valve_bypass_2', 'Valve_heat_2', 'VLV-106-2', 'VLV-112', 'VLV-108'], 
    'flashtank': ['V-100', 'V-101'], 
    'pidfbcontrolop': ['LIC-100', 'LIC-101', 'LIC-102'], 
    'mixerop': ['MIX-100', 'MIX-102', 'MIX-102-2', 'MIX-101', 'MIX-101-2'], 
    'tankop': ['V-102'], 
    'compressor': ['pump_1', 'pump_2'], 
    'teeop': ['TEE-101', 'TEE-101-2', 'TEE-100', 'TEE-100-2', 'TEE-102'], 
    'heatexop': ['E-100', 'E-100-2'],
    'spreadsheetop': ['Pressure boundary condition'], 
    'pipeseg': ['PIPE-101', 'PIPE-102', 'PIPE-100']
}

Case-dependent names

The names of the objects returned by these functions vary depending on the current case opened. A different .usc file will have a completely different set of equipment names, quantities, and even TypeName keys (for example, one case might have no teeop objects at all).

Because of this, the lists in setup.py are specific to one simulation file. If you receive a new .usc file from a colleague, do not assume the old names in setup.py will work — use these utility functions to map out the new case first.
